resources.string: Flatdroid downloads Alpine Linux, then installs Flatpak, a display server (Xvnc and Openbox) and PulseAudio into it. This downloads about 140 MB and needs about 400 MB of storage.
proot can\'t run Alpine on this device: %1$s
Not enough free storage: %1$d MiB free, about %2$d MiB needed
Could not add Flathub with its signing key: %1$s
Your settings are missing; reset to choose them again
Android stopped the setup service (time limit); open Flatdroid to resume
Setup applies these to Flatdroid. You can change them later in Settings.
Only download translations for my languages (%1$s)
Flatpak then skips translations for other languages when it installs and updates apps, which saves space.
(Ctrl-C sent; press X again to force-stop)
Alpine is deleted and set up again from scratch: downloaded again, and its packages reinstalled.
Flatpaks and their data (settings, homes, etc) stay downloaded within Flatdroid to be used again after the environment is reset. Caches are cleared.
Flatpaks and all runtimes are removed, however their data stays (settings, home, etc). Caches are cleared.
Everything in Flatdroid is wiped (Alpine, Flatpak apps and data), and you start from a clean slate. The only thing that remains the same is Flatdroid\'s own global settings.
Alpine environment reset; start setup to install it again.
No apps installed yet. Tap + and enter an app ID from Flathub.
Enter the app\'s ID, as shown on its Flathub page. Separate several IDs with spaces to install them together.
Repairing Flatpak\'s storage after an interrupted task

That can\'t start while an app or a Flatpak task runs.
Not updating: files of %1$s changed since they were installed, and an update would keep them. Start an affected app to reinstall what changed.
Reinstalling didn\'t restore the changed files of %1$s: Flatpak reused its own local copy, which holds the same changes. Don\'t start the affected apps.
An extra-data script changed files of %1$s, which it may not. Reinstall the affected apps and don\'t start them before.
Installs wait until the running app is closed.

Cleaning up old files, this may take a few minute

resources.string: No changed files now: nothing to reinstall.
Determines what the default VNC Viewer app is. With \"Ask every time\", Android asks which app to use each time.
Changes away from the default 30 FPS, significantly increases CPU usage and reduces battery life.
%1$d to %2$d; overrides any other FPS setting. Clear this field to go back to 30/60 FPS.
As many frames as Xvnc can send.
Title bars with close and maximize buttons on app windows. Without them apps get more room, but some (GTK3, Qt) can then only be closed from their own menus.

Lets Flatpak install vendor GPU and video decoding runtimes (NVIDIA, VAAPI) with apps. Flatdroid renders in software and doesn\'t use them; off saves space, and saving with it off removes ones already installed.
Plays sound through Android\'s low latency output instead of its power saving one. Gives less delay and fewer crackles, significantly increases CPU usage and reduces battery life.
Converts sound from apps whose sample rate differs from the phone\'s at a higher quality, slightly increases CPU usage.
%1$d to %2$d; clear the field for the default %3$d ms. Lower is more responsive but can crackle.
Shows extra settings that Flatdroid either manages itself, or are dangerous/unfriendly for the average user.
Some files changed since this app was installed, so it was not started. Another app may have altered them. Reinstall restores the affected packages.
Your answer holds until the app is closed. Swiping this away denies it.
Notifications are off, so Flatdroid can\'t ask when the app records. Your answer holds until the app is closed.
Open it in a VNC viewer at localhost:%1$d
No VNC viewer is installed. Install one (such as AVNC) then connect to the address shown with the password.
Its runtime %1$s is not installed; update or reinstall the app
%1$s is built for %2$s, not %3$s; this app can\'t run here
%1$s was replaced by a link or is missing; not launching. Reinstalling the app recreates it.
The app changed while it was running
The app failed with and without newer Electron\'s flags (exit %1$d)

The size the app\'s screen starts at.

The app doesn\'t ask for sound, turning this on may still work.
When on the first time the app records, a notification asks to allow or deny it until the app is closed. Android\'s microphone is used only while the app records.
Uses Android\'s microphone whenever the app records, without asking.
The app can use the phone\'s cameras whenever it runs, without being asked each time. Works with apps that use Flatpak\'s camera portal. Higher display sizes can cause freezes.
This device has no camera Flatdroid can use.
Android didn\'t allow Flatdroid to use the camera.
\nSome apps don\'t recognize cameras above 30 frames per second. If a camera is missing, it is likely due to this.
Larger sizes use more CPU. The listed resolutions depends on the phone\'s listed resolutions for the chosen frame rate. Cameras that can\'t run at the chosen resolution use the nearest one it can.
Higher rates use more CPU. Only rates this device\'s cameras support are listed. Cameras that can\'t run at the chosen rate use the nearest one it can.
Android didn\'t allow Flatdroid to use the microphone.

This app asks for all devices. Normally it only gets graphics, input, KVM and USB devices where the phone has them. With this on it gets every device node, including Android\'s Binder, through which it can call Android\'s system services as Flatdroid.
One NAME=value per line, added to the app\'s environment over Flatdroid\'s own. Lines starting with # are skipped.
Added after the app\'s own command, separated by spaces. Each is passed as it is: no quoting.
Each line needs NAME=value; names use letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit.
The app is removed, along with runtimes no other app uses unless you keep them.
Also delete its settings, data and files
Keep runtimes no other app uses (update removes them)
Apps set to Shared home use this folder. Without All files access, files other apps put here are hidden from Flatdroid and its apps; bring files in with Import on the home screen.

Flatdroid and apps using the shared home see every file in it, including files other apps put there. It also lets an app have all your shared storage at /sdcard, in its settings. Opens Android\'s setting.
%1$s, shared with every app set to it.
A folder only this app gets, in Flatdroid\'s private storage. Bring files in with "Copy files into private home" under Storage. You can access app private homes through the files app under Flatdroid.
New at every launch, the app\'s settings included, nothing is kept. When the app closes, you can export what it saved.
This app could read, change or delete all your shared files. Flatpaks are not sandboxed.

This installation of Flatdroid didn\'t create %1$s, so files in it from other apps, or from an earlier installation of Flatdroid, are hidden from Flatdroid and its apps.\n\nTo see them, turn on All files access in Settings → Storage. To bring files in, use Import on the home screen. To use another folder, use Change shared home in Settings → Storage.
Choose a folder in Documents or Download on internal storage, or turn on All files access in Settings → Storage to use any folder.
Flatdroid can\'t reach this folder by its path. Choose a folder in Documents or Download on internal storage.
Flatdroid is still copying this app\'s files. Launch it again once that is done.
Couldn\'t create the shared home, %1$s. On Android 10 and older, Flatdroid needs the storage permission for it.
The temporary home is already gone.
The files this app saved are deleted unless you export them. The zip can hold logins the app saved; it goes into Download unless your security settings ask where.
Import a zip into the shared home

The shared hidden files are replaced by the zip\'s.
The shared hidden files are deleted, keys included. Apps that share them start with none.
There are no shared hidden files to export.
The shared hidden files were replaced.
These settings and each app\'s settings in Flatdroid (not the apps\' own settings, which each app\'s Storage section has).
Every setting on this page goes back to its default. Apps\' settings stay.
Its private home is replaced with the contents of a zip you choose next (from Export private home).
Every file in it is deleted. A new, empty one is made when it is next used.
Its settings and other files of its own are replaced with those in a zip you choose next (from Export settings).
Its settings and other files of its own are deleted, as if it had never run. Its home stays.

resources.string: The zip doesn\'t hold Flatdroid settings it can read.
Removes some protections to increase compatibility, and save CPU/memory. Assumes all apps are trusted.
Flatdroid\'s balance of security and performance.
Narrows what apps can reach as far as Flatdroid can: private homes, permissions off until you allow them, fewer devices. Slower, and some apps may lose features.
Your own choice of the settings below. Choosing a level sets them again.
Flatpaks are not sandboxed at any level. Any installed Flatpak can read and change your Flatdroid files and other installed Flatpaks.
You can change each setting a level sets on its own later, in Settings → Security.
App default: block rarely used system calls
Also refuses pidfd_open, process_madvise, kcmp, keyctl, add_key and request_key, which apps rarely need. An app that fails without them can be allowed them in its own settings.
Hide the display and audio processes
Apps can\'t open the memory of Xvnc, Openbox, PulseAudio and the other helpers through /proc. Helper processes started after the app aren\'t covered.
Give apps the permissions they ask for
Also applies to settings still on the default.
If an app asks for permissions, they are granted by default. Off, they start off until you turn them on in an app\'s settings.
The home an app gets until you choose one in its settings. Also applies to apps whose home you haven\'t chosen.
Apps get only CPU and memory information from /sys, and apps asking for all devices get only the basic ones every app has (no GPU, input, KVM or USB devices). Some apps may lose features.
The password shows only when you tap it, the screen can\'t be captured while it\'s shown, and it goes only to the viewer chosen under VNC viewer.
Exports open Android\'s \"save as\" picker instead of going into Download.
App default: share the time zone
App default: share the language and region
App default: share the clipboard with Android

Before an app starts, Flatdroid checks its files against what was recorded when they were installed/updated, to catch possible tampering. It refuses to start an app whose files changed. At most it takes a minute to finish the check. Turning it off drops the recorded baselines, turning it on asks how to record them again.

The installed apps have no baseline yet. Reinstall every app and runtime then record the baselines from the reinstalled files, record them now from the files as they are, or record each app\'s baseline when it first launches.
Reinstalling or recording now can\'t start while an app or a Flatpak task runs.

Lets the terminal run commands while an app runs, and apps start while a command runs. Running apps can take over those commands and run its own code in Alpine\'s proot, with everything Alpine reaches.
These settings change Alpine, which can\'t happen while an app runs. Stop the app, then save again.
An app is running. Stop it first: a command run now could be taken over by the app (see the developer setting \"Terminal while an app runs\").
Commands run behind Flatdroid\'s system call filter, as everything else in Alpine does. Off, tools such as strace and gdb work, and so does anything you run there that tries to leave proot.
Flatdroid couldn\'t make its own process non-dumpable, so an app could read Flatdroid\'s memory. Not starting.
Flatdroid couldn\'t put its system call filter in place, so it started nothing.
This app shows web content without Chromium\'s sandbox: a page it opens can reach everything the app can.
The app asks for sound; your security level keeps it off until you turn it on.
Copy and paste between the app and Android, through the VNC viewer.
The app\'s clock follows Android\'s time zone. Off, the app gets UTC, so its times don\'t hint at where you are.
The app uses Android\'s language, and its region\'s date and number formats, when the app has them. Off, it uses English with generic formats, and can\'t tell your language or region.

Gives the app access to Android\'s fonts for more font compatibility (emojis, other languages). Off, the app has only its runtime\'s fonts, so neither it nor the websites it shows can tell the device\'s Android version and maker from them.
The app asks for network access.
The app asks for network access; your security level keeps it off until you turn it on.
The app doesn\'t ask for network access. Off, it can\'t look up names or open Internet connections.
Lets this app use the system calls your security level blocks (pidfd_open, process_madvise, kcmp, keyctl, add_key, request_key), for an app that fails without them.
Share hidden files and keys with other apps
This app\'s .ssh, .gnupg, shell start-up files and .gitconfig come from one set shared with the other apps that have this on, instead of its own.
Choose a VNC viewer under Settings → VNC viewer first: your security settings don\'t let the password go through Android\'s chooser.
The chosen file can\'t be written.
The zip can hold what apps keep in plain text, such as logins, cookies and keys. In Download, any app with All files access can read it until you delete it.
The zip can hold what apps keep in plain text, such as logins, cookies and keys. Save it where other apps can\'t read it, and delete it once you no longer need it.
